issues.legal_issue: Past cohabitation that had already been exchanged for mutual services did not constitute subsisting consideration for a later promise to transfer property.
material_facts: The transferor and recipient agreed to cohabit and each rendered services to the other pursuant to that agreement.
The recipient's services had been exchanged for the transferor's promise to provide similar services.
The transferor later executed purported sale deeds transferring property to the recipient, and the transfers were motivated by their past cohabitation rather than any future cohabitation.
The transfers were not supported by cash or delivery of jewels.
issues.conclusion: The past cohabitation was the motive, not the consideration, for the later transfers; the transfers were without consideration and were gifts.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 2(d) of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, services that have already operated as consideration for an earlier promise cannot be treated as subsisting consideration for a subsequent promise to transfer property. The judgment distinguished the treatment of past cohabitation in Balo v. Parbati, I.L.R. [1940] All. 370, and Istak Kamu Musalman v. Ranchhod Zipru Bhate, I.L.R. [1947] Bom. 206, 217.

predicates.appeal_over_property_transfer: An appeal concerns a dispute over a transfer of property.
predicates.mutual_cohabitation_services_exchanged: Two people agreed to cohabit and each rendered services to the other pursuant to that agreement.
predicates.services_already_supported_earlier_promi: One person's services were exchanged for the other's earlier promise to provide reciprocal services.
predicates.later_transfer_motivated_by_past_cohabit: A later property transfer was motivated by past cohabitation rather than by an agreement for future cohabitation.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns a property transfer motivated by past cohabitation, and the services rendered in that relationship had already supported an earlier reciprocal promise, those services are not subsisting consideration for the later transfer.

issues.legal_issue: A gift motivated by a desire to compensate a recipient for past cohabitation is not invalid merely because of that motive.
material_facts: The transfers were gifts without consideration, motivated by a desire to compensate the recipient for past illicit cohabitation and services.
Future illicit cohabitation was not the object or consideration for the transfers.
issues.conclusion: The gifts were not hit by section 6(h) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, on the ground that they were motivated by a desire to compensate the recipient for past services.
issues.legal_principle: Section 6(h) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, did not invalidate a gift merely because it was motivated by past cohabitation; the past cohabitation was the motive rather than the consideration or object of the transfer. The Court referred to Balo v. Parbati, I.L.R. [1940] All. 370, and Istak Kamu Musalman v. Ranchhod Zipru Bhate, I.L.R. [1947] Bom. 206, 217, explaining that past cohabitation may be the motive for a gift rather than its consideration.

rule.if: appeal_over_property_transfer and transfer_is_gift and gift_motivated_by_past_cohabitation and no_future_cohabitation_is_object_or_consideration

predicates.appeal_over_property_transfer: An appeal concerns a dispute over a transfer of property.
predicates.transfer_is_gift: The transfer was made without consideration and was a gift.
predicates.gift_motivated_by_past_cohabitation: The gift was motivated by a desire to compensate the recipient for past cohabitation or services.
predicates.no_future_cohabitation_is_object_or_cons: Future cohabitation was neither the object nor the consideration for the transfer.

issues.definition: A gift made to compensate for past cohabitation is not invalid merely for that motive when future cohabitation is not its object or consideration.

issues.legal_issue: Under the applicable Mitakshara law, a coparcener could not gift even his undivided interest in coparcenary property to his concubine.
material_facts: The transferor was governed by the Madras school of Mitakshara law and was the karta of a joint family.
The properties transferred were coparcenary properties.
The recipient was the transferor's concubine.
issues.conclusion: The transferor had no power to make gifts of the coparcenary properties, including his undivided interest, to the recipient, and the gifts were invalid.
issues.legal_principle: Under the Madras school of Mitakshara law, a coparcener had no power to gift even his undivided interest in coparcenary property to his concubine. The Court relied on this rule of Hindu law in holding the gifts invalid.

rule.if: appeal_over_property_transfer and donor_governed_by_applicable_mitakshara_law and property_is_coparcenary_property and recipient_is_donor_concubine and gift_includes_undivided_interest

predicates.appeal_over_property_transfer: An appeal concerns a dispute over a transfer of property.
predicates.donor_governed_by_applicable_mitakshara_: The donor was governed by a Mitakshara rule that restricted gifts of coparcenary property.
predicates.property_is_coparcenary_property: The property transferred belonged to a coparcenary.
predicates.recipient_is_donor_concubine: The recipient was the donor's concubine.
predicates.gift_includes_undivided_interest: The donor purported to gift his undivided interest in the coparcenary property.

issues.definition: A gift of an undivided coparcenary interest to the donor's concubine is invalid when the donor is governed by a Mitakshara rule restricting such gifts.

issues.legal_issue: A later disruption of joint-family status does not validate an earlier invalid gift of coparcenary property without a new gift after disruption.
material_facts: The transferor executed the gifts while the properties were coparcenary property.
The joint family later disrupted and joint status was severed.
After the disruption, the transferor did not make a new gift of his divided interest to the recipient.
issues.conclusion: The later disruption did not validate the earlier invalid gifts; although the transferor could thereafter gift his divided interest, he made no such gift.
issues.legal_principle: An invalid gift of coparcenary property is not validated by a subsequent disruption of the joint family. After disruption, the transferor may make a gift of his divided interest, but a new gift must be made.

rule.if: appeal_over_property_transfer and gift_invalid_when_made_as_coparcenary_property and joint_status_later_severed and no_new_gift_after_severance

predicates.appeal_over_property_transfer: An appeal concerns a dispute over a transfer of property.
predicates.gift_invalid_when_made_as_coparcenary_pr: A purported gift was made while the property was coparcenary property and was invalid when made.
predicates.joint_status_later_severed: The joint family's status was later severed.
predicates.no_new_gift_after_severance: The transferor made no new gift of his divided interest after severance.

issues.definition: When a gift was invalid as a gift of coparcenary property, later severance of joint status does not validate it if the transferor makes no new gift afterward.
